The main executive leader of France's Directory regime from 1795 to 1799, this politician steered the country through the later years of the Revolution — who is he?
Paul Barras: French politician, nobleman and military officer (1755-1829)
Serving two non-consecutive terms as Canada's 15th prime minister, this Quebec-born academic co-founded the journal Cité Libre before entering politics via the Liberal Party — who is he?
Pierre Trudeau: Prime Minister of Canada (1968–1979; 1980–1984)
Educated at Sandhurst in England, this man returned home in 1966 and ruled for nearly half a century, becoming the longest-serving leader in the Arab world at his death — which sultan?
Qaboos bin Said: Sultan of Oman from 1970 to 2020.

Houthi forces in Yemen have launched missiles and drones at shipping tied to Israel amid the Gaza war, drawing military responses from Israel, the US and the UK — what is this ongoing maritime conflict called?
Red Sea crisis: Houthi involvement in the Gaza war. The Red Sea crisis is an ongoing armed conflict and maritime crisis instigated by the Houthis, an armed group in Yemen.
Which retired Italian Army general, elected to the European Parliament for the League in 2024, founded his own far-right party called National Future in 2026?
Roberto Vannacci: Italian military officer and politician (born 1968)

On a single 1929 day in a Chicago garage, seven men were lined against a wall and gunned down — some of the killers disguised as police — in a brutal flashpoint of Prohibition-era gang warfare. What is this killing known as?

Saint Valentine's Day Massacre: 1929 gang shooting in Chicago. The Saint Valentine's Day Massacre was the murder of seven members and associates of Chicago's North Side Gang on Saint Valentine's Day 1929.

It began in August 1999 after Islamist fighters crossed from Chechnya into Dagestan, followed by deadly apartment bombings in Russian cities, and dragged on in the North Caucasus until April 2009 — which conflict?

Second Chechen War: 1999–2009 conflict in Chechnya and the North Caucasus. Russian authorities were quick to blame Chechens for the bombings, although no Chechen, field commander or otherwise, took responsibility for the attacks.
Born Szymon Perski, this Israeli statesman served twice as prime minister and later as president, sitting in the Knesset for 48 years across a 70-year career — who is he?
Known as 'Mother of Modern China,' this wife of Sun Yat-sen became the only female, non-Communist head of state the People's Republic ever had — who was she?
Soong Ching-ling: Wife of Sun Yat-sen (1893–1981)
A former flight attendant who later became a Royal Thai Armed Forces general and the king's bodyguard, she is the fourth wife and current queen of Thailand — who is she?
This Thai telecom tycoon founded the mobile operator AIS, became one of the country's richest people, then won a landslide to become prime minister in 2001 — until a 2006 coup. Who is he?
Thaksin Shinawatra: Prime Minister of Thailand from 2001 to 2006.

Japan's first socialist premier in nearly half a century, this 1990s prime minister is best remembered for an official statement apologizing for his country's past colonial wars on the 50th anniversary of WWII's end. Who was he?
Tomiichi Murayama: Prime Minister of Japan from 1994 to 1996.
This four-star general led Ukraine's Armed Forces as Commander-in-Chief from 2021 until February 2024, then traded the battlefield for the role of Ambassador to the United Kingdom — who is he?
Valerii Zaluzhnyi: Ukrainian general and diplomat (born 1973)

Highly regarded as a military strategist, this Vietnamese general led communist forces to victory across the decades-long Indochina wars, while also serving as minister of defense and deputy prime minister. Who is he?
Võ Nguyên Giáp: Vietnamese general and communist politician (1911–2013)

A paratrooper with Easy Company's 101st Airborne in World War II, this veteran co-wrote a memoir with fellow soldier 'Babe' Heffron and was portrayed by Frank John Hughes in a famed HBO miniseries — who is he?
Serving as head of state under Lenin's new government until his death in 1919, this Bolshevik organizer of the October Revolution also chaired the party's Secretariat — who was he?
Founder of the Pakistan People's Party, this barrister-statesman served as both president and prime minister of Pakistan before his 1977 overthrow and 1979 execution — who was he?
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto: 4th President and 9th Prime Minister of Pakistan (1928–1979)
Which of these four is the eldest?
William Smith (geologist) (born 1769) is the earliest of the four. Financially ruined, Smith spent time in debtors' prison.
Who among these was born first?
Jan Hus (born 1369) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the oldest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Maria Goeppert Mayer is a physicist. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Which of these is a chemist?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele is a chemist. Carl Wilhelm Scheele (German: [ˈʃeːlə], Swedish: [ˈɧêːlɛ]; 9 December 1742 – 21 May 1786) was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist.
What is the atomic number of Livermorium?
Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
What is the atomic number of Polonium?
Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.
In what year was Ferruccio Lamborghini born?
Ferruccio Lamborghini: In 1959, he opened an oil burner factory, Lamborghini Bruciatori, which later entered the business of producing air conditioning equipment.
In what year was Josef Mengele born?
Josef Mengele: Before the war, Mengele received doctorates in anthropology and medicine, and he began a career as a researcher.
In what year did Michael Rockefeller die?
Michael Rockefeller: Michael Clark Rockefeller (May 18, 1938; disappeared November 19, 1961) was an American anthropologist and art collector and member of the Rockefeller family.
In what year did Arthur Schopenhauer die?
Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 – 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.
In what year did Ludwig Wittgenstein die?
Ludwig Wittgenstein: Wittgenstein was born in Vienna into one of Europe's richest families.
In what year was Calcium discovered?
Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.
Which company manufactures Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet?
Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet: McDonnell Douglas. The Super Hornet is in service with the armed forces of the United States, Australia, and Kuwait.
Which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15 from?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15: Soviet Union. The MiG-15 was one of the first successful jet fighters to incorporate swept wings to perform near Mach 1.
Who is credited with discovering Molybdenum?
Molybdenum: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
Who is credited with discovering Serotonin?
Serotonin: Arda Green. It is involved in mood, cognition, reward, learning, memory, and physiological processes such as vomiting and vasoconstriction.
Who is credited with discovering Beryllium?
Beryllium: Louis Nicolas Vauquelin. Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
Stretching from the thoracic diaphragm to the pelvic brim, this body region sits between the chest and the pelvis — which body part?
Abdomen (also belly or stomach in vertebrates, or metasoma in arthropods) is the front part of the torso between the thorax (chest) and pelvis in humans and in other vertebrates.

This Austrian psychotherapist founded a school of psychology emphasizing birth order and belonging, breaking from Freud by proposing that contributing to others is key to a person's sense of worth — who is he?
Alfred Adler (Austrian; February 7, 1870 - May 28, 1937) was an Austrian medical doctor, psychotherapist, and founder of the school of individual psychology.
This joint region where the foot meets the leg comprises three joints built from the talus, tibia, and fibula, enabling the foot's up-and-down flexing motions — what body part is it?
Ankle is the area where the foot and the leg meet.
This American physicist won a share of the 1927 Nobel Prize for an effect, now bearing his name, that demonstrated light's particle nature — who was he?
Arthur Compton (September 10, 1892 - March 15, 1962) was an American physicist who shared the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics with C. T. R. Wilson.
Grown for its edible taproot in red or golden varieties and closely related to Swiss chard, this vegetable's leaves are eaten too, sold simply as "greens" — which root vegetable?
Beetroot is the taproot portion of a Beta vulgaris subsp.
Ranging from southern Canada down to Oaxaca, Mexico, this North American wild cat sports black bars on its forelegs and a short, bobbed tail. What animal is it?
Bobcat (Lynx rufus), also known as the wildcat, bay lynx, or red lynx, is one of the four extant species within the medium-sized wild cat genus Lynx.
Located between the lower back and the perineum, these two rounded regions of human anatomy are built around the gluteus maximus — the largest muscle in the human body — name this body part?
Buttocks (sing.: buttock) are two rounded portions of the exterior anatomy of humans, located on the posterior of the pelvic region.
This root vegetable owes its typical orange color to beta-carotene, though heirloom varieties can be white, purple, or even black — what vegetable is it?
Originating in Northern China, this spitz-type dog breed is known for a dense double coat that forms a distinctive ruff around the neck — name the breed?
Chow Chow is a spitz-type of dog breed originally from Northern China.
Though it resembles a barn swallow, this medium-sized bird is actually more closely related to hummingbirds than to any swallow, its resemblance being pure convergent evolution — what bird is it?

Common swift (Apus apus) is a medium-sized bird, superficially similar to the barn swallow or house martin but somewhat larger, though not stemming from those passerine species, being in the order Apodiformes.
This transdisciplinary field studies circular causal processes like feedback and recursion, where an action's outcome becomes the input for the next — what field is it?
Cybernetics is the transdisciplinary study of circular causal processes such as feedback and recursion, where the outcomes of actions return as inputs for subsequent actions.

This gut ailment flares up when small pouches in the wall of the large intestine become inflamed, often striking with sudden lower-abdominal pain — fever or bloody stool warns of a complication; what is it?
Diverticulitis is a gastrointestinal disease characterized by inflammation of abnormal pouches - diverticula - that can develop in the wall of the large intestine.
This mammal family includes living species from two genera as well as extinct giants like the woolly mammoth, and was first scientifically described in 1821 — what family is it?

Elephantidae is a family of large, herbivorous proboscidean mammals which includes the living elephants (belonging to the genera Elephas and Loxodonta), as well as a number of extinct genera like Mammuthus (mammoths) and Palaeoloxodon.
Known regionally in Shropshire as the 'plum bird,' this small European finch, scientifically Pyrrhula pyrrhula, was the original bird to carry its common English name — which species?
Eurasian bullfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula) is a small passerine bird in the finch family, Fringillidae.
Systematically named methanal and carrying the formula CH2O, this pungent gas turns up in particle board, disinfectants, and lab specimen jars — what is it?

Formaldehyde (for-, US also fr-) (systematic name methanal) is a pungent colorless gas mainly used in the production of industrial resins, such as for particle board, coatings, plastics, pulp, paper, synthetic fibers, and textiles.
Nicknamed 'The Lawyer' and celebrated for his eccentric style, this principal shareholder controlled over 4% of Italy's entire GDP through his automaker — who was he?
Gianni Agnelli (12 March 1921 - 24 January 2003), nicknamed L'Avvocato ('The Lawyer'), was an Italian industrialist and principal shareholder of Fiat.
Born Herman Webster Mudgett, this con artist and killer worked his crimes around the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, earning the nickname "the Beast of Chicago" — who was he?
H. H. Holmes (May 16, 1861 - May 7, 1896), better known as Dr.
With species ranging from evergreen trees to climbing shrubs across the tropics and temperate zones, this genus's most iconic species decorates Christmas cards worldwide — what genus is it?
Holly is a genus of over 570 species of flowering plants in the family Aquifoliaceae, and the only living genus in that family.

This nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug treats pain, fever, and inflammation — from migraines to arthritis — and typically starts working within an hour, whether taken orally or intravenously. What drug?
Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.

This American scientist co-authored a landmark 1953 paper with Francis Crick proposing the double-helix structure of DNA, building on research by Rosalind Franklin, and shared a 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery — who is he?
James Watson (April 6, 1928 - November 6, 2025) was an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist.
This Soviet-designed naval helicopter has spawned variants for assault transport, export, and civilian use, and still flies today from Russia to India -- which aircraft?

Kamov Ka-27 (NATO reporting name 'Helix') is a military helicopter developed for the Soviet Navy, and as of 2024 is in service in various countries including Russia, Ukraine, Vietnam, China, South Korea, and India.
Closely related to earthworms but equipped with a sucker at each end, these segmented parasitic or predatory worms make up their own subclass within the annelid phylum — what are they?
Leech are segmented parasitic or predatory worms that comprise the subclass Hirudinea within the phylum Annelida.
Based on a commercial airliner design, this four-engine turboprop aircraft hunts submarines for the U.S. Navy using a distinctive tail-mounted magnetic detector — what plane is it?
Lockheed P-3 Orion is a four-engined, turboprop anti-submarine and maritime surveillance aircraft developed for the United States Navy and introduced in the 1960s.

With over 2,400 species sporting triangular heads, bulging eyes on flexible necks, and folded forelegs built to snatch prey, these insects count termites and cockroaches among their closest relatives — what are they?
Mantis are an order (Mantodea) of insects that contains over 2,400 species in about 460 genera in 33 families.
This field of study examines and evaluates the procedures researchers use to gather and interpret data, rather than the findings those procedures produce — what is it called?
Methodology is the study of research methods.

Sharing the insect order Lepidoptera with butterflies but typically sporting duller, darker wing patterns, this group includes roughly 160,000 mostly nocturnal species, many still undescribed by science — name this group of insects?
Moth are a group of winged insect of the order Lepidoptera, the other well-known members of which are butterflies, they are characterized by dark or dull patterned wings.

This Renaissance polymath put the Sun, not the Earth, at the center of the universe in a 1543 book published just before his death — likely arriving independently at an idea Aristarchus of Samos had floated eighteen centuries earlier. Who is he?
Nicolaus Copernicus (19 February 1473 - 24 May 1543) was a Renaissance polymath who formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center.
Fossils of these arachnids in 400-million-year-old Scottish rock look startlingly modern — colloquially they're called harvestmen or daddy long legs. What order is this?
Opiliones (formerly Phalangida) are an order of arachnids, colloquially known as harvestmen, harvesters, daddy long legs, or granddaddy long legs.
This English amateur astronomer joined an astronomy association at age 11, compiled the Caldwell catalogue, and hosted the BBC's record-breaking 'The Sky at Night' — who was he?
Patrick Moore (4 March 1923 - 9 December 2012) was an English amateur astronomer who attained prominence in that field as a writer, researcher, radio commentator and television presenter.
This bird genus, part of the flamingo family Phoenicopteridae, encompasses the living flamingo species — which genus?
Phoenicopterus is a genus of birds in the flamingo family Phoenicopteridae.
Named from the Greek for an infinite carbon chain it would ultimately become, this class of organic compounds strings together alternating single and triple bonds. What is it called?
Polyyne is any organic compound with alternating single and triple bonds; that is, a series of consecutive alkynes, (CC)n with n greater than 1.

Also called blepharoptosis and sometimes mistakenly called 'lazy eye,' this condition is marked by the drooping of the upper lid over the eye and can affect vision development in children if untreated — what is it?
Ptosis (eyelid) is a drooping or falling of the upper eyelid.
This inflammatory disease typically develops two to four weeks after a streptococcal throat infection and can damage the heart valves in about half of cases — what is it?
Rheumatic fever (RF) is an inflammatory disease that can involve the heart, joints, skin, and brain.
This grayish-leaved, purple-flowered evergreen subshrub is a Mediterranean member of the mint family, long used both as a culinary herb and an ornamental garden plant — what plant is it?
Salvia officinalis is a perennial, evergreen subshrub, with woody stems, grayish leaves, and blue to purplish flowers.
Until 2010, this pungent little cultivar of the onion was classified as its own species before being folded back into the common onion — name this allium?
Shallot is a cultivar group of the onion. Until 2010, the (French red) shallot was classified as a separate species, Allium ascalonicum.
This circular muscle normally maintains constriction of a natural body passage, relaxing only as physiological function requires — what is it called?
Sphincter is a circular muscle that normally maintains constriction of a natural body passage or orifice and relaxes as required by normal physiological functioning.
Among the most experienced spacewalkers in history, this NASA astronaut logged over 62 hours across nine spacewalks — the most of any woman — who is she?
Sunita Williams (ne Pandya; born September 19, 1965) is a retired United States Navy captain and former NASA astronaut.
What academic discipline studies religious belief from within a faith perspective, focusing on the nature of divinity, revelation, and the history behind organized religion?
Theology is the study of religious belief from a religious perspective, with a focus on the nature of divinity and the history behind religion.
Caused by a single-celled parasite and often symptom-free, this common STI can be diagnosed by examining vaginal fluid under a microscope or with a DNA test — what is it?
Trichomoniasis (trich) is an infectious disease caused by the parasite Trichomonas vaginalis.

Native to Europe and parts of Asia, this parasitic plant draws water and nutrients from host trees and has long featured in European mythology, now commonly used in Christmas decorations — what is it?
Viscum album is a species of mistletoe in the family Santalaceae, commonly called European mistletoe, common mistletoe, or simply mistletoe (Old English mistle).
Making up just 1% of described fungal species, these single-celled eukaryotes reproduce by budding or fission and usually measure a mere 3–4 micrometers across — what are they?
Yeast is any species of fungus that grows primarily in a unicellular form and reproduces via budding or fission.
Caused by excess growth hormone after the body's growth plates have closed, this disorder first shows up as enlarged hands and feet before affecting the jaw and forehead — what condition is it?
Acromegaly: Human disease that results in excess growth of certain parts of the body.
Also called the Persian silk tree or mimosa tree, this flowering species in the pea family is native to Asia — what is it?

Albizia julibrissin: Species of plant. Albizia julibrissin, the Persian silk tree, pink silk tree, or mimosa tree, is a species of tree in the Fabaceae family, native to southwestern and eastern Asia.
Despite being named after a European bird for its reddish-orange breast, this thrush is the most abundant landbird on its continent, numbering some 370 million individuals — what is it?
American robin: Species of bird. The American robin (Turdus migratorius) is a migratory bird of the true thrush genus and Turdidae, the wider thrush family.
Nicknamed "the heart of the scorpion," this reddish supergiant is the brightest star in its constellation — what is it?
Antares: Binary star in the constellation Scorpius.
Sold under the brand name Abilify, this atypical antipsychotic treats schizophrenia, bipolar mania, and irritability linked to autism spectrum disorder — what is it?
Aripiprazole: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Aripiprazole is taken by mouth or via injection into a muscle.
From the Greek for "self-devouring," this lysosome-driven process lets a cell tidily break down and recycle its own worn-out parts — what is it?
Autophagy: Process of cells digesting parts of themselves.
Spurred by the 1980 failure of Operation Eagle Claw, this American tiltrotor blends a helicopter's vertical takeoff with a turboprop's long-range cruise — what aircraft is it?
Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey: Military transport tiltrotor.
Rich in vitamin C and polyphenols, this deciduous shrub's glossy dark berries are cooked into jams and syrups or fermented into cassis — what is it?
Blackcurrant: Species of flowering plant in the gooseberry family Grossulariaceae.

This infraorder of decapod crustaceans tucks a stubby tail-like abdomen under a hard shell and ends its front pair of legs in pincers — over 1.5 million tonnes of them are eaten by humans yearly. What group is it?
Brachyura: Crustacean. The true crabs are the largest of the crab decapod groups with carcinised body forms.
A cole crop related to broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, the heaviest recorded head of this leafy vegetable weighed nearly 138 pounds — what is it?
Cabbage: Leafy vegetable in the flowering plant family Brassicaceae.
This infraorder of decapod crustaceans is the true taxonomic home of what everyone actually calls a shrimp, found in fresh and salt water worldwide — what is it?
The largest part of the brain, this structure houses the cerebral cortex plus the hippocampus and basal ganglia, and works with the cerebellum to control every voluntary action. What is it?
Cerebrum: Large part of the brain containing the cerebral cortex.
This Dutch scientist discovered Saturn's largest moon and invented the pendulum clock, the most accurate timekeeper for nearly three centuries — who is he?
Christiaan Huygens: Dutch mathematician and physicist (1629–1695)
Nicknamed the 'palm thief,' this giant terrestrial arthropod can weigh over 9 pounds, making it the largest land-dwelling arthropod alive today — what is it?
Thanks to a variation in the gene OR6A2, some people taste this herb — called cilantro in the US — as fresh and citrusy while others swear it tastes like soap. What is it?
Coriander: Annual herb. Coriander, or Coriandrum sativum, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.
Once sold under the brand name Flexeril and chemically similar to tricyclic antidepressants, this oral medication treats sudden muscle spasms — what's the drug?
Cyclobenzaprine: Muscle relaxant medication. It should not be used together with MAOIs.
Caused by about 40 types of fungus and often picked up in public showers or contact sports like wrestling, this infection produces a red, itchy, scaly circular rash — what is it?
Dermatophytosis: Fungus infection of the skin. Dermatophytosis, also known as tinea and ringworm, is a fungal infection of the skin (a dermatomycosis), that may affect skin, hair, and nails.

Originally developed to compete for a USAF aerial-tanker contract it lost to Boeing's Stratotanker, this four-engined jetliner instead entered airline service with Delta in 1959 — what aircraft was it?
Douglas DC-8: American four-engined jet airliner family.
Capable of delivering shocks up to 860 volts, this South American knifefish helped inspire the invention of the battery in 1800 — what is it?
Electric eel: Genus of fishes in South America.
Also called rocket or arugula, this sharp-flavored leaf vegetable native to the Mediterranean and Asia is a popular salad green in the cabbage family — which plant?
This burrowing mammal builds ever-expanding tunnel systems, and its saliva contains toxins that paralyze its favorite prey, earthworms — what animal is it?
European mole: Species of mammal. The European mole (Talpa europaea) is a mammal of the order Eulipotyphla.
Historically used in the 18th century to track down escaped slaves, this large Brazilian dog breed of mastiff type now also serves as a guard dog and companion — which breed?
Fila Brasileiro: Brazilian breed of dog. The Fila Brasileiro (Portuguese pronunciation: [ˈfilɐ bɾaziˈlejɾu]) is a Brazilian breed of large working dog of mastiff type.
Also called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon or Red Car Theory, this cognitive bias makes you notice something everywhere right after you first learn about it — what is it?
Frequency illusion: Kind of cognitive bias. The name "Baader–Meinhof phenomenon" was coined in 1994 by Terry Mullen in a letter to the St.
This mathematician founded set theory and proved that there are more real numbers than natural numbers, revealing an infinity of infinities — who is he?
This plant genus in the mallow family gives us cotton, humanity's primary natural fiber, with its name tracing to an Arabic word for a soft substance — which genus?
Gossypium: Genus of flowering plants in the mallow family Malvaceae.

Derived independently in the 1830s by two European researchers and later given theoretical backing by George Stokes, this law describes the pressure drop of laminar flow through a drinking straw or a hypodermic needle — what's it called?
Hagen–Poiseuille equation: Law describing the pressure drop in an incompressible and Newtonian fluid.
Introduced to Britain in the 19th century as an ornamental plant, this Caucasus-native's sap causes painful blistering burns when exposed skin meets sunlight — which species?
Heracleum mantegazzianum: Species of flowering plant. Heracleum mantegazzianum, commonly known as giant hogweed, is a monocarpic perennial herbaceous plant in the carrot family Apiaceae.

In the Renaissance this field of study covered classical literature and language rather than religion or divinity, and today it groups subjects using critical and interpretive methods rather than empirical ones — what broad academic category is this?
Humanities: Academic disciplines that study society and culture.

Dubbed the 'saviour of mothers,' this Hungarian doctor proved in 1847 that hand-washing with chlorinated lime solutions could drastically cut deadly childbed fever at a Vienna maternity clinic — who is he?
Ignaz Semmelweis: Early pioneer of antiseptic procedures.
Native to South America but planted worldwide for its long-lasting violet blooms, this tree — also called the black poui — is listed as Vulnerable in its wild range by the IUCN. What is it?
Jacaranda mimosifolia: Species of sub-tropical tree.
This British physicist shared the 1951 Nobel Prize with Ernest Walton for first splitting the atomic nucleus — a feat that opened the way to nuclear power and weapons. Who was he?
Defined by a carbon-oxygen double bond flanked by two carbon groups, this class of organic compound includes acetone and gives some sugars and steroids like testosterone their structure — what is it?
Ketone: Organic compounds of the form >C=O.
At Bologna in the 1700s she became the first woman to hold a science doctorate and the first salaried female university teacher — depicted as the goddess Minerva herself; who was she?
Laura Bassi: Italian physicist and academic (1711–1778)
This soft, movable pair of appendages on the jaw helps with eating and speech, and is often used in kissing — what are they?
Lip: Visible body parts at the mouth.
Named from the Latin for "wolf," this autoimmune disease often announces itself with a red facial rash and alternates between flares and remission — what is it?
Lupus: Autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue.
Boiled down from its sap to make a beloved breakfast syrup, this genus of roughly 132 tree and shrub species counts the sycamore as its type species — which genus of trees?
Made up of the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater, these three protective membranes shield the brain and spinal cord while containing cerebrospinal fluid — what are they called?
Meninges: Three membranes protecting the brain. In anatomy, the meninges (sing. meninx; from Ancient Greek μῆνινξ (mêninx) 'membrane') are protective membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord.
This Russian polymath discovered the atmosphere of Venus and formulated the law of conservation of mass, while also helping shape the modern Russian literary language as a poet — who is he?
With roughly 200 species across 16 genera, this family of elongated fish is almost exclusively marine, with a name traced back through Portuguese and Latin to a Greek word — which family?
Moray eel: Family of fishes. Moray eels, or Muraenidae, are a family of eels whose members are found worldwide.
Sold as Narcan, this opioid antagonist can restore breathing within minutes of an overdose but may trigger sudden withdrawal in opioid-dependent people — what is it?
Naloxone: Opioid receptor antagonist. Naloxone, sold under the brand name Narcan among others, is an opioid antagonist, a medication used to reverse or reduce the effects of opioids.
What is this — “Index of chemical compounds with the same name”?
Nitrogen oxide: Index of chemical compounds with the same name. Nitrogen oxide may refer to a binary compound of oxygen and nitrogen, or a mixture of such compounds:.
Named after the Greek word for tumor, first used this way by the physician Galen nearly two millennia ago, this medical field focuses on diagnosing and treating cancer — what is it called?
Oncology: Branch of medicine dealing with, or specializing in, cancer.
This condition inflames a large organ behind the stomach, sending severe upper-abdominal pain into the back, with chronic cases bringing weight loss and fatty stool — what is it?

Caused by a lack of vitamin B3 (niacin), this disease is remembered for its grim quartet of symptoms — inflamed skin, diarrhea, dementia, and mouth sores — striking sun-exposed skin first. What is it?
Pellagra: Human disease caused by a lack of vitamin B3. The two main types of pellagra are primary and secondary.
Formed by stripping three protons from phosphoric acid, this triply-charged ion carries the formula PO4³⁻ and lends its name to esters like trimethyl ester in organic chemistry — what anion is it?
Phosphate: Anion, salt, functional group or ester derived from a phosphoric acid.
Brightly colored as a warning sign, these diurnal tropical amphibians of Central and South America brew their toxicity from a diet of ants, mites, and termites — what's this group of frogs?
Poison dart frog: Family of amphibians.

Derived from arachidonic acid and containing a distinctive 5-carbon ring among its 20 carbons, this lipid compound can trigger opposite effects in different body tissues. What hormone-like substance is it?
Prostaglandin: Group of physiologically active lipid compounds.
Its thick bark gets harvested every 9 to 12 years for wine-bottle stoppers and cricket-ball cores — what species of oak, native to southwest Europe and Africa, is this?
Quercus suber: Species of plant. Quercus suber, commonly called the cork oak, is a medium-sized, evergreen oak tree in the section Quercus sect.
Striking children recovering from a viral illness like the flu, this brain disease has been linked in about 90% of cases to aspirin use — what is it called?
Reye syndrome: Rapidly worsening brain disease.
Discovered in 1861 via flame spectroscopy by Bunsen and Kirchhoff, this alkali metal is named from the Latin word for 'deep red' — which element?
Rubidium: Chemical element with atomic number 37 (Rb)
Caused by the same Group A strep behind strep throat, this childhood illness brings a sandpapery red rash and a bumpy tongue — what is it?
An adult female of this ruminant is a ewe, a castrated male a wether, and a young one a lamb — and with about 1.2 billion of them, they're easily the most common of their kind. What animal?
